analysis.one_liner: Nearly triples federal tobacco taxes and bans flavored tobacco, including menthol cigarettes and vapes.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action in either chamber and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would roughly triple the federal cigarette tax, from about $1.01 to $3.00 per pack, and raise taxes on cigars, smokeless tobacco, pipe tobacco, roll-your-own tobacco, and other products to similar per-use rates so users cannot switch to a cheaper alternative. It would tax e-cigarettes at the cigarette-equivalent rate, ban characterizing flavors in tobacco products — including menthol in cigarettes and flavored vapes — unless the Health Secretary finds a specific vape flavor helps adults quit without attracting young users, and authorize $500 million a year for the CDC's Office on Smoking and Health.
analysis.who_benefits: People who quit smoking or never start — especially teenagers, who are the most price-sensitive users and the main target of flavored products — along with public health generally and the CDC's anti-smoking programs, which would be funded at $500 million a year.

how_it_helps.text: The federal cigarette tax would rise from $50.33 to $150 per thousand cigarettes — from about $1.01 to $3.00 per pack — and higher prices are the most proven way to cut smoking, with young users the most sensitive to price.

Cigars, smokeless tobacco, pipe tobacco, and roll-your-own tobacco would all be raised to comparable per-use tax rates, closing the loopholes that let users shift to cheaper products to avoid a cigarette tax increase.

The bill bans characterizing flavors — including menthol, mint, strawberry, grape, and vanilla — in all tobacco products starting one year after enactment, targeting the flavors used to attract young users.
It would tax e-cigarettes and other FDA-regulated nicotine products at a cigarette-equivalent per-use rate for the first time, closing the gap that made vaping the cheap flavored option.
It authorizes $500 million a year for the CDC's Office on Smoking and Health, which runs anti-smoking and youth-prevention programs.
Tax rates would rise with inflation each year, so the price deterrent keeps pace rather than eroding over time.

analysis.who_pays: People who keep using tobacco, who would pay roughly triple the current federal tax — a burden that falls hardest on lower-income smokers who don't quit. Tobacco manufacturers, e-cigarette companies, and retailers would bear sharply reduced sales plus a one-time tax on inventory on hand the day after enactment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Smokers who don't quit, and tobacco firms

drawbacks.text: Tripling the federal cigarette tax to about $3.00 per pack would cost a pack-a-day smoker roughly $730 more per year if they do not quit; tobacco taxes are regressive, hitting lower-income smokers hardest, and the increase takes effect the day after enactment with no phase-in.
A one-time floor stocks tax would force anyone holding tobacco inventory on the day after enactment to immediately pay the difference between the old and new tax on that stock.

Banning menthol and flavored vapes removes products some adult smokers use to switch away from cigarettes, though the bill gives the Health Secretary authority to approve specific vape flavors shown to significantly help cessation without attracting young users.
Steep tax increases on tobacco can push some sales into illicit channels, a cost that falls on enforcement and honest retailers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is well-designed for its purpose: tax parity across products, an inflation index, a flavor ban, and CDC funding attack youth nicotine use from several directions at once. The serious honest objection is the regressive hit on lower-income smokers who do not quit — an abrupt tripling of the federal tax with no phase-in — plus the disruption of an immediate inventory tax on retailers. On balance, the public health gains (fewer teenage nicotine addicts, fewer smoking deaths over time) outweigh the costs, but the burden is unevenly distributed.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees, then a Health subcommittee the next day, and neither committee ever voted on it before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Suozzi introduced the bill on September 19, 2019, joined by five original cosponsors.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and on September 20, 2019, to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee.
No further action was ever taken: no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote in either chamber before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco companies and e-cigarette makers kept the status quo — no tax increase and flavored products, including menthol, remained on the market. Smokers kept paying the old tax rate, and the public continued to bear the health costs of nicotine addiction.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's five cosponsors split four Democrats and one Republican, but it never reached a floor vote, so its partisan support was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would nearly triple the federal cigarette tax to $3.00 per pack and raise every other tobacco product to a similar per-use rate, ending the low-tax status quo the industry depends on. Its interest in keeping prices down runs directly against the public health goal of reducing smoking.

Vaping products would be taxed at a cigarette-equivalent per-use rate for the first time, and characterizing flavors would be banned unless the Health Secretary finds a flavor significantly helps adult smokers quit without attracting youth. The industry argues flavored vapes help adults switch from cigarettes, but flavored products also drove the surge in teen vaping the bill targets.

Higher taxes would cut tobacco sales, and a one-time floor stocks tax would force retailers to immediately pay the tax difference on inventory held the day after enactment. Their revenue depends on continued tobacco consumption, which conflicts with the bill's public health purpose.
